### Questions

`docs` and `anno` hold 200 AG News articles, 50 each labeled `"Business"`,
`"Sci/Tech"`, `"Sports"`, or `"World"`, drawn deterministically from the
benchmark's held-out test partition. Each row of `docs` is one short wire
article: a `doc_id`, its true topic `label`, and the raw `text` sent by a
news service. This corpus differs from both the Wikipedia author pages the
chapter uses for its TF-IDF examples and the IMDb reviews of the last two
notebooks, and it has a mess of its own. Several articles still carry a
literal backslash where the original source wrapped a line, fusing two words
together with no space between them. A later question deals with that mess
directly. Print results unless a question says otherwise.

1. Filter `anno` to alphabetic tokens, group by `lemma`, and count. Print the
15 most frequent lemmas in the whole corpus.

```{python}
(
    anno
    .filter(c.is_alpha)
    .group_by(c.lemma)
    .agg(count = pl.len())
    .sort(c.count, descending=True)
    .head(15)
)
```

2. Look at the list from question 1. How many of these 15 words have
anything to do with business, technology, sports, or world news?

None of them. Every entry is a determiner, preposition, conjunction, or
auxiliary verb, plus `say`, the verb every wire story uses to attribute a
quote, and two wire-service names (`AP`, `Reuters`) that describe where the
article came from, not what it is about. This is a sharper version of the
chapter's "publisher" example. With IMDb, the raw frequency list at least
surfaced `movie` and `film` near the top, because every review was about the
same kind of thing. AG News mixes four unrelated subjects by design, so a
corpus-wide raw count has no single dominant noun. Separating the four topics
takes weighting by document frequency, which is the point of TF-IDF.

3. Compute the TF-IDF table with `DSText.compute_tfidf(anno, min_df=0.01, max_df=1.0)`,
matching the chapter's own call. Then build the top-10-terms-per-document
table the same way the chapter does, and print its shape.

```{python}
tfidf = DSText.compute_tfidf(anno, min_df=0.01, max_df=1.0)

top_terms = (
    tfidf
    .sort([c.doc_id, c.tfidf], descending=[False, True])
    .group_by(c.doc_id)
    .head(10)
    .group_by(c.doc_id)
    .agg(top_lemmas = c.lemma.str.join("; "))
)
top_terms.shape
```

4. Pick two articles from each label (eight total, the first two `doc_id`s
within each label) and print their `top_lemmas` alongside the true `label`.
Before checking the `label` column, try to guess each article's topic from
its term list alone.

```{python}
sample_docs = (
    docs
    .sort(c.label, c.doc_id)
    .group_by(c.label, maintain_order=True)
    .head(2)
    .select(c.doc_id, c.label)
)

(
    top_terms
    .join(sample_docs, on=c.doc_id)
    .select(c.doc_id, c.label, c.top_lemmas)
    .sort(c.label, c.doc_id)
)
```

Some of these give themselves away immediately. `doc120027`'s list
(`Phelps`, `Gold`, `medley`, `medal`, ...) is plainly Sports, and
`doc120033`'s (`chief`, `Canadian`, `Press`, `police`, `custody`, ...) reads
as World news before you check. Others are harder. `doc120028` is Sports too,
but three of its ten top terms (`he`, `his`, `that`) are the kind of function
word question 2 found filling the raw frequency count, and TF-IDF has not
fully removed them here.

5. Investigate the backslash artifact. In the first block, flag each of the
200 raw articles for whether its `text` contains a literal `\` character,
group by `label`, and report the count `n` and the proportion `pct_backslash`
per label, sorted by proportion descending. In the second block, print the
`doc_id` and `text` of the first article whose text contains a `\`.

```{python}
(
    docs
    .with_columns(has_backslash = c.text.str.contains(r"\\"))
    .group_by(c.label)
    .agg(n = pl.len(), pct_backslash = c.has_backslash.mean())
    .sort(c.pct_backslash, descending=True)
)
```

```{python}
(
    docs
    .filter(c.text.str.contains(r"\\"))
    .select(c.doc_id, c.text)
    .row(0, named=True)
)
```

23 of the 200 articles carry the artifact, from 20% of Business articles
down to none in Sports. That reflects how the source copy was formatted, not
what the articles are about. `doc120042`'s text shows the effect: `"hoping
their\back-to-school fashions"` glues `their` to `back-to-school` with no
space, and spaCy's tokenizer marks the fused token `their\back` as
non-alphabetic. All 65 fused tokens in the corpus get the same treatment, so
none of them appear in question 1 or question 3. The `is_alpha` filter that
both `DSText.compute_tfidf` and a plain word count rely on drops them without
an error or a warning, and a real word from each original sentence never
reaches either table.

6. For the words `he`, `his`, `who`, `they`, `at`, `with`, `for`, `that`,
`AP`, `Reuters`, and `AFP`, compute what proportion of the 200 documents
each one appears in.

```{python}
candidates = ["he", "his", "who", "they", "at", "with", "for", "that", "AP", "Reuters", "AFP"]

(
    anno
    .filter(c.is_alpha)
    .group_by(c.lemma)
    .agg(n_docs = c.doc_id.n_unique())
    .with_columns(df_prop = c.n_docs / 200)
    .filter(c.lemma.is_in(candidates))
    .sort(c.df_prop, descending=True)
)
```

None of these reaches 40% document frequency (`for` comes closest at 39%),
and `he`, `who`, and `they` sit at about 10% or below. The book's `max_df`
example works because "publisher" appears on almost every Wikipedia
biography; here, a `max_df` cutoff anywhere above 0.4 would leave every word
on this list untouched. In a topically diverse news corpus, pronouns and
prepositions do not have to appear in many documents to be uninformative.
They only have to be common within one short document, and document
frequency cannot measure that.

7. Redefine what counts as a "document." Join `label` onto `anno`, drop the
original `doc_id`, and rename `label` to `doc_id`, so every article sharing
a topic is now treated as one pooled document. Recompute TF-IDF on this
table with `max_df=0.75`, and print the top 10 terms for each of the four
categories. In the second block, plot the same top 10 terms per category as
a bar chart with `geom_col()` and `coord_flip()`, faceting by `doc_id` with
free scales.

```{python}
anno_cat = (
    anno
    .join(docs.select(c.doc_id, c.label), on=c.doc_id)
    .drop("doc_id")
    .rename({"label": "doc_id"})
)

cat_tfidf = DSText.compute_tfidf(anno_cat, min_df=0.0, max_df=0.75, doc_name="doc_id")

top_cat = (
    cat_tfidf
    .sort([c.doc_id, c.tfidf], descending=[False, True])
    .group_by(c.doc_id)
    .head(10)
    .group_by(c.doc_id)
    .agg(top_lemmas = c.lemma.str.join("; "))
)
top_cat
```

```{python}
plot_terms = (
    cat_tfidf
    .sort([c.doc_id, c.tfidf], descending=[False, True])
    .group_by(c.doc_id)
    .head(10)
)

(
    plot_terms
    .ggplot(aes("lemma", "tfidf"))
    .geom_col()
    .coord_flip()
    .facet_wrap("doc_id", scales="free")
    .labs(title="Top 10 TF-IDF Terms by AG News Category", x="Term", y="TF-IDF")
)
```

8. Compare this category-level list to question 4's per-article lists. Does
pooling all 50 articles into one document surface anything that wasn't
already visible at the single-article level?

Some of it was already there: `doc120027`'s top-10 list had `Phelps`,
`Gold`, and `medal`, and the pooled Sports list adds `olympic` and `Athens`,
the same event seen from a wider angle. But the Sci/Tech list (`IBM; some;
service; network; company; I; he; Linux; Mars; include`) is not something
any single sample article predicted. No article in question 4 mentioned
IBM, Linux, or Mars, because each of those subjects dominates only a handful
of the 50 Sci/Tech articles. The chapter's line that "the result depends on
how we define a document" is literal here: treating 50 articles as one
document changes which words count toward `tf`, changes `N` from 200 to 4,
and gives a different and more useful picture of each category. Pooling
does not solve the pronoun problem from question 4, though. `he`, `his`, and
`I` still turn up in three of the four category lists, because with only
four pooled documents a word has to appear in all four to exceed the 0.75
cutoff.
